name: Cross-legged
summary: The classic shins-crossed seat. A cushion can make it friendlier; knees do not have to reach the ground. “Easy pose” is a name, not a promise.
demands: Hip external rotation (the knees fall out, not the ankles up)
A pelvis that can stay upright rather than rolling back
cues: Sit near the front of a firm cushion; adjust the height until it feels comfortable
Let the knees rest where they fall; add support beneath them if useful
Cross the shins loosely rather than forcing feet underneath thighs
Change the front leg or choose another position when you want
cautions: Stop or adjust for knee or hip pain, tingling, or numbness; do not press the knees down
If floor transfers feel uncertain, begin on a stable higher seat and ask for guidance

name: Kneeling
summary: A kneeling seat with the hips toward the heels. A bench or cushion changes the depth and pressure. Lovely for some knees; absolutely optional for others.
demands: Knee flexion and ankle plantarflexion (pointing the toes back)
Tolerance for weight through the front of the shins
cues: Slide a seiza bench or a firm cushion between your heels to take the load off the ankles and knees
Let the sit-bones rest down; lengthen up through the crown
Point the toes straight back, not tucked
Come out and shake the legs the moment they tingle
cautions: Tingling or numbness is a cue to change position, not a harmless sensation to endure. Get advice if it persists or recurs.
Deep knee bending and pointed ankles may be unsuitable with pain, injury, or postoperative restrictions. Choose a different seat.

name: Resting squat
otherName: Supported squat · heels raised if useful
summary: Hips lower toward your heels while your feet and a sturdy support help you balance. Depth is personal. A shallow supported version is a perfectly good version.
demands: Ankle, knee, and hip range that varies with stance, body proportions, and depth
Balance and a controlled way to lower and rise
cues: Hold a secure support. Use a stable, non-slip heel wedge if it helps; avoid loose stacks of books
Choose a comfortable stance and toe angle rather than copying an exact shape
Lower only as far as comfortable; allow the knees to follow the direction of your feet
Make the visit brief, then use your support to stand
cautions: Prolonged occupational or habitual squatting is a different exposure from a brief supported practice; the research does not establish a safe duration for everyone
Skip painful ranges and follow your care team’s restrictions after injury or surgery
props: A wall or door frame to hold

name: Long-sitting
summary: Legs out in front, with as much knee bend and back support as you want. A simple change from folded-leg positions, and a useful option when deep knee bending is unwelcome.
demands: Hip flexion with comfortable knee positioning
Enough seat height or back support to relax rather than brace
cues: Sit on a firm cushion or lean against a supportive surface
Bend the knees as much as feels good; a rolled blanket underneath may help
Let your trunk settle into a comfortable position instead of forcing it upright
Change position if a pulling sensation becomes painful or tingly
cautions: Do not force straight knees or stretch through radiating pain, tingling, or numbness. Persistent symptoms need assessment.

name: Side-sitting
summary: Both legs folded to one side: a cosy option for conversation or play, with a hand or cushion for support. Switch sides if comfortable; perfect symmetry is not an entrance requirement.
demands: External rotation in the front hip, internal rotation in the back hip
cues: Let the whole pelvis settle; don't perch on one buttock
Keep the ribs stacked over the hips rather than collapsing sideways
Deliberately switch to the other side every few minutes
Use a hand or cushion to level the low hip
cautions: The two hips do different things here. Try another position if one side is uncomfortable rather than forcing symmetry.
Ease off if either knee hurts or you notice tingling.

name: Between the heels
summary: A deeper kneeling variation with the seat between the feet, usually raised on a block or bolster. A specialist item on the menu, not the final boss of floor sitting.
demands: Deep knee flexion with tolerance for the tibia rotating
cues: Sit up on a block or bolster placed between the feet — never force the hips to the floor
Keep the feet pointing straight back, not splaying out
Lengthen up; let the thighs and ankles stretch, not the knees
Build tolerance with short holds
cautions: This asks for considerable knee flexion. Skip it with knee pain, injury, or restrictions on deep bending.
Never push the hips down or twist through knee pain. Use a higher support or another position.
goodFor: A tall, stable seat once available
props: Block or bolster between the feet
